newsitem.title: RUSSIA: IMF leaves Moscow without finishing assessment.
newsitem.headline: IMF leaves Moscow without finishing assessment.

text.p: An International Monetary Fund (IMF) mission left Russia on Friday without completing an assessment of the economy which would enable the Fund to decide whether to pay out delayed instalments of a $10 billion loan, the IMF's Moscow representative said.
Tom Wolf told Reuters that local staff, in contact with IMF Washington headquarters, would continue to work on the review of the economy over the next few days, now the mission had left.
"It wasn't able to complete its assessment during the mission... We don't know how soon the assessment will be completed but I would say in a few working days," he said.
The main areas the mission was looking at were fiscal issues, especially tax collection, pension and wage arrears, and structural reforms of the economy, he said.

The mission has also made progress on a detailed programme under the three-year loan for 1997, he said. It will return in mid-February with the aim of finishing work on the 1997 programme and to conduct the next regular review of the economy.
The loan aims to help Russia weather the pain of moving to a market economy and start growing again after several years of contraction, while preventing inflation from taking off.

The Fund last year repeatedly delayed payments of the loan, known as an Extended Fund Facility, largely because Russian tax collection was running far below budgeted levels, threatening to undermine government finances.
Just as many companies have not been settling each other's bills or paying taxes to the state, the government has fallen behind in paying public-sector wages and pensions.
IMF lending resumed at the end of 1996, but two monthly tranches, of about $330 million each, have still not been paid, apart from the January instalment on which the assessment is still open.
Sources close to the talks between the Russian government and Fund experts said tax collection had continued to improve in December.

The Russians are hoping that if the latest assessment turns out to be positive, and the Fund continues to pay the loan, they will receive the two delayed tranches in one go, something the sources said was realistic.
But before the IMF agrees to a programme for this year, it will want to see a realistic 1997 budget in place.
The State Duma lower house of parliament was giving the 1997 budget its fourth and final reading on Friday, but a large number of minor amendments dragged the debate into the evening.
